questions.stimulusTitle: A Second Life for City Rain
questions.stimulusText:
In many cities, rainwater flows from roofs and pavement into storm drains. During heavy storms, the drainage system may fill faster than it can empty. One method of reducing this strain is the rain garden: a shallow planted area designed to collect runoff temporarily.
A rain garden is usually placed lower than nearby hard surfaces. Water enters it through a channel or opening and spreads across soil planted with grasses, flowers, and shrubs. The garden does not remain a pond. Instead, its layers allow water to soak gradually into the ground. Plant roots create small pathways in the soil, and leaves slow the force of falling rain.
Rain gardens can also trap some sediment before it reaches streams. Yet their location and construction matter. A garden built too close to a foundation may direct moisture toward a building. Soil that drains very slowly may require a special underlayer or another solution entirely. For this reason, planners first study the site's slope, soil, and typical rainfall.
Although one rain garden cannot prevent every flood, many small gardens distributed across a neighborhood can reduce the amount of water entering drains at the same moment. They turn overlooked spaces into working parts of a city's water system.

questions.stimulusText:
When people speak together, silence is often treated as an empty space that someone should quickly fill. A pause, however, can do useful work. It gives a listener time to consider what has been said, and it gives a speaker time to choose an accurate response rather than the fastest one.
Different settings give pauses different meanings. During a performance, a brief silence may create suspense. In a classroom discussion, it may signal that students are still forming ideas. In a conversation between friends, it can show careful attention. Of course, silence can also result from confusion or discomfort. Its meaning depends on what happens before and after it.
Because rapid replies are often praised as signs of confidence, people may fear that pausing makes them appear uncertain. Yet a quick response is not always a thoughtful response. Skilled interviewers sometimes wait after an answer instead of rushing to the next question. The person being interviewed may then add a detail that would otherwise have remained unspoken.
Learning to tolerate a short silence does not mean avoiding conversation. It means recognizing that communication includes timing as well as words. A pause is not necessarily the absence of meaning; sometimes it is the space in which meaning becomes clearer.

questions.stimulusText:
Nico had practiced the opening notes of his cello solo until his fingers moved without hesitation. Yet during the final rehearsal, a rattling sound followed every low note. He checked the strings, adjusted his chair, and began again. The rattle returned.
Across the empty auditorium, custodian Ms. Bell paused beside a heating vent. “Play that phrase once more,” she called. When Nico did, she walked slowly along the front row and stopped at a music stand. A loose pencil on its shelf trembled whenever the cello's low notes filled the room.
Nico removed the pencil and laughed with relief. Then Ms. Bell asked him to repeat the phrase. This time the sound was clear, but Nico noticed that he had rushed the final measure. He played it again, listening more carefully than before.
The next evening, the auditorium was crowded. Nico could not see Ms. Bell from the stage, but he remembered how patiently she had searched for the small disturbance. Instead of hurrying through the difficult measure, he let each note settle before beginning the next. When the final note faded, the room remained silent for one breath—and then the applause began.

Seed coats provide one form of dormancy. A hard coat may block water until weather, soil particles, or an animal's digestion weakens it. Other seeds contain chemical controls that change only after a period of cold. Such seeds may fall in autumn but wait through winter before sprouting. By spring, the cold requirement has been met, and young plants face a longer growing season.
Dormancy does not guarantee survival. A seed may still land where there is too little sunlight or where animals can eat it. However, dormancy spreads risk over time. Seeds from the same plant do not always sprout together; some may wait months or even years. If drought destroys one group of seedlings, later seeds may encounter better conditions.
Farmers and gardeners sometimes imitate natural processes to end dormancy. They may gently scratch a hard seed coat or keep certain seeds in a cool, damp place for several weeks. These methods do not force growth by themselves. They remove a barrier so that a seed can respond when other needs are met.

Before inexpensive printed books became common, producing a book required extensive labor. Scribes copied words by hand, and other workers prepared pages, bindings, and colored decorations. Because books were valuable, owners sometimes recorded more than the main text on their pages.
Notes written in margins are called marginalia. A reader might define an unfamiliar word, disagree with an argument, mark an important passage, or record when the book was purchased. Some notes are no more than quick symbols. Others form a conversation across generations: one reader responds to the text, and a later reader responds to the earlier note.
For historians, marginalia can reveal how people actually used a book. A spotless volume may show what information was available, but an annotated one can show which ideas attracted attention. Still, researchers must be cautious. A name written inside a cover does not always identify the person who made every note, and handwriting can be difficult to date.
Modern readers also write beside texts, whether on paper or with digital annotation tools. The technology has changed, but the impulse is familiar. Readers do not merely receive words; they question, connect, and select. A margin may look like unused space, yet it can preserve evidence of an active mind meeting a text.

questions.stimulusText:
When the clock above the town hall stopped, everyone noticed. Its hands pointed stubbornly to 2:17, and people crossing the square began checking their phones. Mr. Imani, who repaired clocks in a narrow shop nearby, was asked to inspect it. He invited his niece Leila to carry the tool case.
Inside the tower, Leila expected to find a broken gear. Instead, every brass wheel appeared whole. Mr. Imani wound the mechanism and listened. A faint scrape sounded, paused, and sounded again. Rather than opening the largest section, he followed the rhythm to a thin metal arm near the bell.
A single screw had loosened. Each time the arm moved, it brushed another piece and slowed the mechanism. Leila handed over a screwdriver, and Mr. Imani tightened the screw by half a turn. The gears stirred, and the minute hand advanced.
“That was all?” Leila asked as the bell marked the next hour.
“Small causes can make loud problems,” he replied.
On the way down, Leila carried the case more carefully. It no longer seemed like a box of tools. It seemed like a collection of ways to pay attention.

questions.stimulusText:
For the school storytelling night, Amara arranged twelve chairs in a semicircle. Twelve children had registered, so twelve chairs seemed exact. Then she noticed a boy lingering near the doorway with his father. He had no name tag and kept glancing toward the empty stage.
Amara found another chair in the hallway and placed it at the end of the row. Her teammate Jonah frowned. “If we keep changing the plan, we'll start late,” he whispered.
Before Amara could answer, a family entered with two registered children and their younger sister. The sister sat in the extra chair while the boy at the doorway remained standing. Amara brought a second chair. Soon another child arrived unexpectedly, and Jonah silently went to the hallway himself.
When the first storyteller began, the semicircle was uneven and crowded. Yet no one stood at the doorway. During the final story, Jonah leaned toward Amara. “Next time,” he said, “we should plan for more than the plan.”
Afterward, the boy's father explained that they had only intended to listen from the hall. His son had been nervous about entering. The extra chair, he said, had felt like an invitation.

A fallen tree may look like forest waste, but it can become a busy habitat. Once a trunk lies on the ground, fungi begin breaking down its wood. Their threadlike structures spread through cracks and release substances that help decompose tough plant material.
As the wood softens, insects tunnel beneath the bark. These tunnels create spaces where moisture collects. Salamanders and other small animals may shelter in the cool, damp areas, while birds search the log for insects. Mosses sometimes grow on the surface and hold additional water.
Decomposition also returns nutrients to the soil. The process is gradual: a large trunk may take decades to become part of the forest floor. questions.prompt: What allowed distant weather measurements to be compared quickly?

choices.A: Printed atlases
choices.B: Satellite photographs
choices.C: Weather balloons
choices.D: Telegraph networks

questions.correctAnswer: Telegraph networks
questions.explanation: Telegraph systems carried observations from distant towns to a central office quickly.
questions.stimulusText:
Before satellites photographed storms, weather information traveled by message. In the nineteenth century, expanding telegraph networks allowed observers in different towns to report temperature, wind, and air pressure to a central office. For the first time, measurements taken far apart could be compared soon after they were recorded.
Workers plotted the reports on maps. When similar air-pressure readings were connected, patterns appeared across regions. A single observation could describe only one place, but a map assembled from many observations could show the movement of a weather system. These early maps did not provide the detailed forecasts people expect today, yet they made short-term warnings more practical.
The system had limits. Instruments were not always calibrated alike, messages could arrive late, and large areas had few reporting stations. Mapmakers had to decide how much confidence to place in incomplete information. They revised maps as new reports arrived rather than treating the first version as final.
This work established an important principle of modern forecasting: useful predictions depend not only on gathering data but also on combining observations from many locations. Technology has transformed the speed and scale of that work, but the need to connect separate measurements remains.
